subject: physics

items.q: Which observation from photoelectric experiments cannot be explained by the classical wave theory of light?
items.correct: Photoelectrons are emitted without any measurable delay, even in very dim light.
items.misconception: More photoelectrons are emitted each second when the light is made much more intense.
items.why: Students learn the photon explanation of each feature and then list all of them as evidence, without asking what the wave model would predict for the same experiment. The step of comparing the predictions of two models is the one that is skipped. A result is evidence for one model over another only if the two models predict different outcomes. A wave model also predicts that more intense light, delivering more energy per second, releases more electrons per second, so this result does not distinguish the models. The discriminating results are the threshold frequency, the independence of E_max from intensity and the absence of a time delay.
items.specStatementText: the photoelectric effect as evidence of the particle nature of light
items.random_wrong: More photoelectrons are emitted each second when the frequency of the light is raised.

items.q: A student argues: 'When the intensity of light above the threshold frequency is doubled, the photocurrent doubles. This result proves that light consists of photons.' Which evaluation of this argument is correct?
items.correct: It is flawed: a wave model also predicts that more intense light releases more photoelectrons each second.
items.misconception: It is flawed: the photocurrent depends on the frequency of the light, not on its intensity.
items.why: 'Frequency' sounds like 'how often', so students link it with the number of events per second, and 'intensity' sounds like 'strength', so they link it with energy. Research on the photoelectric effect has documented students swapping the roles of frequency and intensity in exactly this way. The energy of each photon is hf, so the frequency sets the maximum kinetic energy, E_max = hf − Φ. The intensity of light of one frequency sets the number of photons arriving per second, so it sets the number of photoelectrons per second and the photocurrent.
items.specStatementText: the photoelectric effect as evidence of the particle nature of light
items.random_wrong: It is valid: a wave model cannot explain why a more intense beam releases more photoelectrons.

items.q: Which statement defines the threshold frequency of a metal?
items.correct: The lowest frequency of light that can release photoelectrons from the metal
items.misconception: The maximum frequency of light that can release photoelectrons from the metal
items.why: Everyday experience of water and rope waves links 'bigger' waves with more energy, and students picture a long wavelength as a large wave. Many also confuse the threshold frequency (a minimum) with the threshold wavelength (a maximum) because both are called 'threshold'. E = hf = hc/λ: photon energy is proportional to frequency and inversely proportional to wavelength. Violet photons (about 400 nm) carry more energy than red photons (about 650 nm). Photoelectrons are released only by radiation of frequency ABOVE f₀, which means wavelength BELOW λ₀ = hc/Φ.
items.specStatementText: that photons of a certain frequency, known as the threshold frequency, are required to release photoelectrons from the metal
items.random_wrong: The frequency of light that releases the most photoelectrons per second from the metal

items.q: Sodium has a work function of 2.28 eV. Light from a 50 mW red laser of wavelength 650 nm, and then light from a dim violet lamp of wavelength 400 nm delivering only 0.10 mW, falls on a clean sodium surface. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Which light releases photoelectrons from the sodium?
items.correct: Only the violet light, despite its lower power
items.misconception: Both the red light and the violet light
items.why:
This is exactly what the classical wave model, in which energy arrives continuously across the wavefront, predicts, and it matches everyday experience of things warming up gradually in sunlight. Students who have learned the wave model of light apply it here. Energy is absorbed in whole photons, one photon per electron. If hf < Φ, no single photon can free an electron, and the energy absorbed does not accumulate in the electron to release it later. Above the threshold, emission starts with no measurable delay even in very dim light, because one photon is enough.

Working: Red: E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(650 × 10⁻⁹ m) = 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = (3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) eV = 1.91 eV < 2.28 eV, so no emission at any power. Violet: E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)(3.00 × 10⁸)/(400 × 10⁻⁹) = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.11 eV > 2.28 eV, so photoelectrons are emitted (E_max = 3.11 − 2.28 = 0.83 eV). Equivalently, λ₀ = hc/Φ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)(3.00 × 10⁸)/(2.28 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 5.45 × 10⁻⁷ m = 545 nm; only wavelengths shorter than this release electrons.
items.specStatementText: that photons of a certain frequency, known as the threshold frequency, are required to release photoelectrons from the metal
items.random_wrong: Only the red light, from the 650 nm laser
items.working: Red: E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(650 × 10⁻⁹ m) = 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = (3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) eV = 1.91 eV < 2.28 eV, so no emission at any power. Violet: E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)(3.00 × 10⁸)/(400 × 10⁻⁹) = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.11 eV > 2.28 eV, so photoelectrons are emitted (E_max = 3.11 − 2.28 = 0.83 eV). Equivalently, λ₀ = hc/Φ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)(3.00 × 10⁸)/(2.28 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 5.45 × 10⁻⁷ m = 545 nm; only wavelengths shorter than this release electrons.

items.q: Ultraviolet radiation of wavelength 200 nm falls on a clean zinc plate. The work function of zinc is 4.30 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the stopping potential for the photoelectrons?
items.why:
Students remember E = hf as 'the energy the electron gets' and forget that the electron is bound in the metal. The step from E = hf to E_max = hf − Φ is often not connected to the idea of the energy needed to escape. Energy conservation for one photon and one electron: hf = Φ + E_max for the least tightly bound electrons. Different metals have different work functions, so the same light gives different values of E_max from different metals, and none at all if hf < Φ.

Working: hf = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(200 × 10⁻⁹ m) = 9.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. In eV: 9.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ J / 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ = 6.22 eV. E_max = hf − Φ = 6.22 eV − 4.30 eV = 1.92 eV. eV_s = E_max, so V_s = 1.92 V.
items.specStatementText: Einstein’s explanation using the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons as given by E_max = hf − Φ where Φ is the work function of the metal

items.q: For each of two metals, P and Q, a student plots the maximum kinetic energy E_max of the photoelectrons against the frequency f of the incident light. Both graphs are straight lines. The line for P meets the frequency axis at 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and the line for Q meets it at 7.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Which statement about the two lines is correct?
items.correct: They have equal gradients, each equal to the Planck constant h.
items.misconception: Q's line is steeper, because its gradient is set by the larger work function.
items.why: Students recognise that the graphs for different metals differ and assume every feature of the line changes. They also look for Φ in the gradient because the gradient is usually the quantity asked for. Compare E_max = hf − Φ with y = mx + c: the gradient is h and the y-intercept is −Φ. For every metal the gradient is the same universal constant h, so the lines for different metals are parallel; a larger work function shifts the line to a higher threshold frequency.
items.specStatementText: Einstein’s explanation using the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons as given by E_max = hf − Φ where Φ is the work function of the metal
items.random_wrong: Each line shows the kinetic energy of every photoelectron at that frequency.

items.q: Monochromatic light falls on the emitting plate of a photocell. The potential of the collecting electrode relative to the emitting plate is varied. The photocurrent is zero at −1.2 V and below; it rises as the potential increases and levels off at 3.0 μA above about +2 V. The intensity of the light is then doubled, with its frequency unchanged. Which describes the new current–potential graph?
items.correct: The current is zero at −1.2 V and below, as before, and levels off at 6.0 μA.
items.misconception: It becomes zero only at a more negative potential, and levels off at 6.0 μA.
items.why:
In everyday experience and in the classical wave picture, a brighter or stronger source does more: louder sound, bigger water waves, more heating. Physics-education research on the photoelectric effect has repeatedly found students attributing to intensity the effects of frequency, and predicting that the stopping potential rises with intensity. Intensity sets the number of photons arriving per second, not the energy of each photon (E = hf). Each electron absorbs one photon, so E_max = hf − Φ is unchanged when intensity alone increases, and so is the stopping potential. What increases is the number of photoelectrons per second, and so the saturation current.

Working: At a fixed frequency each photon has the same energy hf, so E_max = hf − Φ is unchanged and the stopping potential is still 1.2 V (the current is zero at −1.2 V). Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons, and so of photoelectrons, per second: saturation current = 2 × 3.0 μA = 6.0 μA.
items.specStatementText: Einstein’s explanation using the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons as given by E_max = hf − Φ where Φ is the work function of the metal
items.random_wrong: It becomes zero only at a more negative potential, and still levels off at 3.0 μA.
items.working: At a fixed frequency each photon has the same energy hf, so E_max = hf − Φ is unchanged and the stopping potential is still 1.2 V (the current is zero at −1.2 V). Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons, and so of photoelectrons, per second: saturation current = 2 × 3.0 μA = 6.0 μA.

items.q: In an electron diffraction tube, electrons accelerated through a potential difference of a few kilovolts pass through a thin film of graphite and strike a fluorescent screen, where bright concentric rings are seen. How does this experiment provide evidence for the wave nature of matter?
items.correct: The rings are a diffraction pattern, at angles that fit a wavelength λ = h/p for the electrons.
items.misconception: The rings form where electrons bounce off the carbon atoms like balls, at particular angles.
items.why: Students meet the electron as a small charged particle in atomic models and circuits, and Rutherford scattering shows particles being deflected by atoms, so a particle-deflection explanation seems natural. Particle deflections would not produce sharp rings at angles that depend on the electrons' momentum. The ring angles obey the diffraction condition for waves of wavelength h/p; increasing the accelerating potential difference increases p, shortens λ and shrinks the rings. Uncharged particles such as neutrons, atoms and molecules also diffract.
items.specStatementText: diffraction of particles as evidence of the wave nature of matter
items.random_wrong: Electrons in the beam interfere with one another beyond the film, and the rings mark where they reinforce.

items.q: In an electron diffraction tube the accelerating potential difference is 3.0 kV and one of the rings on the screen has a radius of 24 mm. The accelerating potential difference is increased to 6.0 kV. Assume the electrons are non-relativistic and that the radius of the ring is proportional to the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons. What is the new radius of this ring?
items.correct: 17 mm
items.misconception: 12 mm
items.why:
Students meet E = hc/λ first and it links energy and wavelength directly, so they reuse it for every quantum object. Both formulas contain h, and both are described as 'wavelength of a quantum object'. For a photon, p = E/c, so λ = h/p = hc/E. For a particle of mass m moving slowly compared with c, p = √(2mE_k), not E_k/c. So λ = h/√(2mE_k), which is proportional to 1/√E_k, not 1/E_k, and depends on the mass.

Working: E_k = eV, so p = √(2m_e eV) and λ = h/√(2m_e eV) ∝ 1/√V. With r ∝ λ: r_new = r × √(V₁/V₂) = 24 mm × √(3.0 kV/6.0 kV) = 24 mm/√2 = 17 mm.
items.specStatementText: diffraction of particles as evidence of the wave nature of matter
items.random_wrong: 34 mm
items.working: E_k = eV, so p = √(2m_e eV) and λ = h/√(2m_e eV) ∝ 1/√V. With r ∝ λ: r_new = r × √(V₁/V₂) = 24 mm × √(3.0 kV/6.0 kV) = 24 mm/√2 = 17 mm.

items.q: In a scattering experiment, a beam of high-energy electrons, each of momentum 2.24 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹, is directed at a thin carbon target. The intensity of the electrons scattered by the carbon nuclei is measured at different angles to the beam, and the first minimum of intensity is found at 51°. Assume the first minimum occurs at the angle θ where sin θ ≈ λ/D, where λ is the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons and D is the diameter of a nucleus. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. What is the estimated diameter of a carbon nucleus?
items.why:
Resolving vectors uses sine and cosine interchangeably depending on which angle is chosen, so students learn that 'either can appear' and do not check which one a given formula needs. Use the function in the formula with the angle it defines. Here θ is measured from the original direction of the beam and the first minimum satisfies sin θ ≈ λ/D.

Working: λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)/(2.24 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹) = 2.96 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. sin θ ≈ λ/D, so D ≈ λ/sin θ = (2.96 × 10⁻¹⁵ m)/sin 51° = (2.96 × 10⁻¹⁵ m)/0.777 = 3.8 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.
items.specStatementText: diffraction of particles as evidence of the wave nature of matter

items.q: What is meant by the statement that matter exhibits wave–particle duality?
items.correct: Particles such as electrons show wave behaviour, such as diffraction, in some experiments and particle behaviour in others.
items.misconception: Particles such as electrons remain particles, but they travel through space along wave-shaped paths.
items.why: Diagrams draw a wave as a sinusoidal line, and students picture a particle following that line. Research on students' ideas about quantum objects has found this 'wavy trajectory' picture to be common. Wave–particle duality means that the electron's behaviour is described by a wave whose interference and diffraction determine where it is likely to be found, while each electron is detected at a single point. There is no wavy trajectory; the wave is not a path in space.
items.specStatementText: that matter exhibits wave–particle duality
items.random_wrong: Only the smallest particles, such as electrons, have a wave nature; objects such as dust grains are purely particles.

items.q: Electrons are sent towards a double slit at such a low rate that only one electron is in the apparatus at any time. Each electron is recorded as a single dot on a detector screen. At first the dots seem to be scattered at random, but after many thousands of electrons they form a pattern of bright and dark fringes. What do these results show about each electron?
items.correct: It is detected at one point, like a particle, but wave interference sets where it is likely to land.
items.misconception: It is deflected by the electrons that went through before it, and this builds up the fringes over time.
items.why: For water or sound waves, interference is described as two waves meeting, so students assume two electrons must meet to interfere. Research on students' understanding of the double-slit experiment with electrons has documented this interpretation. Experiments in which only one electron is in the apparatus at a time still produce the full pattern once many electrons have been recorded. The pattern is a property of each electron's wave, which describes where it is likely to be detected; it does not need other electrons to be present.
items.specStatementText: that matter exhibits wave–particle duality
items.random_wrong: It follows a wavy path from the slits, which carries it to one of the bright fringes.

items.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 2.0 kV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and treat the electron as non-relativistic. What is the de Broglie wavelength of the electron?
items.why:
The factor ½ in E_k = ½mv² is a well-known point of error, and it is easily lost when the expression is rearranged to give momentum. Start from E_k = ½mv² and p = mv: p² = m²v² = 2m × ½mv² = 2mE_k, so p = √(2mE_k) and λ = h/√(2mE_k).

Working: E_k = eV = (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(2.0 × 10³ V) = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁶ J. p = √(2m_eE_k) = √(2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg × 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁶ J) = 2.41 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹. λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)/(2.41 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹) = 2.7 × 10⁻¹¹ m.
items.specStatementText: the de Broglie wavelength for particles as given by λ = h/p

items.q: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy, and both move at speeds much less than c. The mass of the proton is about 1830 times the mass of the electron. How do their de Broglie wavelengths compare?
items.correct: The electron's wavelength is about 43 times the proton's.
items.misconception: The proton's wavelength is about 43 times as long as the electron's.
items.why:
Students associate 'more' of a particle with 'more' of its wave, and the inverse proportionality in λ = h/p is easy to reverse when not written down. The de Broglie wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum. Increasing the accelerating potential difference increases the electrons' momentum and shortens their wavelength; a proton with the same kinetic energy as an electron has more momentum and a shorter wavelength.

Working: λ = h/p and p = √(2mE_k). With equal E_k: λ_e/λ_p = √(2m_pE_k)/√(2m_eE_k) = √(m_p/m_e) = √1830 = 42.8 ≈ 43.
items.specStatementText: the de Broglie wavelength for particles as given by λ = h/p
items.random_wrong: The electron's wavelength is about 1830 times the proton's.
items.working: λ = h/p and p = √(2mE_k). With equal E_k: λ_e/λ_p = √(2m_pE_k)/√(2m_eE_k) = √(m_p/m_e) = √1830 = 42.8 ≈ 43.

items.q: A cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg is bowled at 30 m s⁻¹ towards a gap several metres wide between two fielders. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Which statement explains why no diffraction of the ball is observed?
items.correct: Its de Broglie wavelength is far too short compared with the width of the gap.
items.misconception: It has no de Broglie wavelength, since it is not a subatomic particle.
items.why:
The wave nature of matter is taught only through electrons and other subatomic particles, and students never see a large object diffract, so they conclude the idea does not apply to it. λ = h/p applies to any object with momentum. A 0.16 kg ball at 30 m s⁻¹ has λ ≈ 10⁻³⁴ m, far smaller than any gap or obstacle, so its diffraction is unobservable. Diffraction has been observed for electrons, neutrons, atoms and large molecules.

Working: p = mv = 0.16 kg × 30 m s⁻¹ = 4.8 kg m s⁻¹. λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)/(4.8 kg m s⁻¹) = 1.4 × 10⁻³⁴ m, about 10³⁴ times smaller than a gap of a few metres.
items.specStatementText: the de Broglie wavelength for particles as given by λ = h/p
items.random_wrong: It is uncharged, and only charged particles such as electrons diffract.
items.working: p = mv = 0.16 kg × 30 m s⁻¹ = 4.8 kg m s⁻¹. λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)/(4.8 kg m s⁻¹) = 1.4 × 10⁻³⁴ m, about 10³⁴ times smaller than a gap of a few metres.

items.q: In Compton's experiment, X-rays of a single known wavelength were scattered by electrons in a block of graphite, and the wavelengths of the scattered X-rays were measured at several angles. Which result is evidence for the particle nature of light?
items.correct: The scattered X-rays included a longer wavelength, shifted by an amount that increased with angle.
items.misconception: The scattered X-rays all had the same wavelength as the incident X-rays, at every angle.
items.why: Reflected light keeps its colour, and a ball bouncing elastically off a fixed wall keeps its speed. The classical wave model also predicts no change of wavelength, because an electron driven by a wave re-radiates at the driving frequency. An electron is not a fixed wall: it recoils and takes some of the photon's energy and momentum. The scattered photon therefore has less energy and a longer wavelength. The observed shift, which follows the collision prediction Δλ = (h/m_e c)(1 − cos θ), is the evidence for photons.
items.specStatementText: Compton scattering of light by electrons as additional evidence of the particle nature of light
items.random_wrong: X-rays were scattered in all directions, as balls would be when they hit a target.

items.q: When an X-ray photon is scattered by a free electron, the scattered photon has a longer wavelength than the incident photon. What is the reason?
items.correct: The photon transfers some of its energy to the recoiling electron, so its energy hc/λ decreases.
items.misconception: The photon loses some of its speed in the collision, which stretches its wavelength.
items.why: For material particles, less kinetic energy means lower speed, and students transfer this to photons, picturing them as tiny balls that are slowed by a collision. The energy of a photon is E = hf = hc/λ, and its speed in a vacuum is c whatever its energy. Losing energy lowers f and raises λ at the same speed c.
items.specStatementText: that photons scatter off electrons with increased wavelength
items.random_wrong: Some photons are absorbed, so the scattered beam is weaker and has a longer wavelength.

items.q: X-rays of wavelength 7.10 × 10⁻¹¹ m are Compton scattered by free electrons. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the wavelength of the X-rays scattered through an angle of 120°?
items.why:
The symbol Δ is sometimes read as 'initial minus final', and students who associate a collision with a decrease subtract the shift without checking the direction. The scattered photon has less energy, so a longer wavelength. The formula defines Δλ = λ_f − λ_i, which is never negative since 1 − cos θ ≥ 0, so λ_f = λ_i + Δλ.

Working: h/(m_ec) = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)/(9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg × 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m. Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos 120°) = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m × (1 − (−0.50)) = 3.64 × 10⁻¹² m. λ_f = λ_i + Δλ = 7.10 × 10⁻¹¹ m + 0.364 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 7.46 × 10⁻¹¹ m.
items.specStatementText: the shift in photon wavelength after scattering off an electron as given by λ_f − λ_i = Δλ = (h/m_e c)(1 − cos θ).

items.q: Photons are Compton scattered by free electrons. For which scattering angle θ is the increase in the wavelength of the photons greatest?
items.correct: θ = 180°, where the photon is scattered straight back
items.misconception: θ = 90°, where the photon turns at right angles
items.why:
Students treat 90° as the 'largest' deflection because it is perpendicular, and many sine-based results peak at 90°. At 90° the shift equals h/m_e c, which makes 90° seem special. The photon's change of momentum, and so the energy given to the electron, is greatest when it rebounds straight back. 1 − cos θ is 1 at 90° and 2 at 180°.

Working: Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ). 1 − cos θ ranges from 0 (θ = 0°) through 1 (θ = 90°) to 2 (θ = 180°), so the shift is greatest at θ = 180°: Δλ_max = 2h/m_ec = 2 × 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m = 4.85 × 10⁻¹² m.
items.specStatementText: the shift in photon wavelength after scattering off an electron as given by λ_f − λ_i = Δλ = (h/m_e c)(1 − cos θ).
items.random_wrong: θ = 0°, where the photon carries straight on
items.working: Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ). 1 − cos θ ranges from 0 (θ = 0°) through 1 (θ = 90°) to 2 (θ = 180°), so the shift is greatest at θ = 180°: Δλ_max = 2h/m_ec = 2 × 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m = 4.85 × 10⁻¹² m.

items.q: X-rays of wavelength 7.1 × 10⁻¹¹ m and visible light of wavelength 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m are each scattered through 90° by free electrons. The Compton shift is easily measured for the X-rays but not for the visible light. Take h/(m_ec) = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m. What is the reason?
items.correct: The shift is the same for both, but it is a tiny fraction of the visible wavelength.
items.misconception: The shift is far smaller for visible light, as visible photons carry much less energy.
items.why:
Students know that a high-energy photon loses more energy in a collision than a low-energy one and assume the wavelength shift scales in the same way; the fact that the shift is observed only with X-rays seems to confirm it. Separate the change in wavelength from the change in energy. Δλ depends only on θ, but the energy lost, hc/λ − hc/(λ + Δλ), is much larger when λ is short. For visible light the same Δλ is a negligible fraction of λ, so the shift cannot be measured.

Working: Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos 90°) = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m × 1 = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m for both. Fraction of X-ray wavelength: 2.4 × 10⁻¹²/7.1 × 10⁻¹¹ = 0.034 (3%). Fraction of visible wavelength: 2.4 × 10⁻¹²/5.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 4.8 × 10⁻⁶ (about 0.0005%).
items.specStatementText: the shift in photon wavelength after scattering off an electron as given by λ_f − λ_i = Δλ = (h/m_e c)(1 − cos θ).
items.random_wrong: Visible light is scattered only as a wave, since just high-frequency radiation acts as photons.
items.working: Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos 90°) = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m × 1 = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m for both. Fraction of X-ray wavelength: 2.4 × 10⁻¹²/7.1 × 10⁻¹¹ = 0.034 (3%). Fraction of visible wavelength: 2.4 × 10⁻¹²/5.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 4.8 × 10⁻⁶ (about 0.0005%).

items.q: The photoelectric effect shows that light delivers its energy in quanta of energy hf. A student claims that Compton scattering simply confirms this and gives no additional evidence for the particle nature of light. Which statement about Compton scattering is correct?
items.correct: It shows that a photon also carries momentum h/λ, exchanged with one electron in a collision that conserves momentum and energy.
items.misconception: It shows that X-rays consist of photons, whereas the photoelectric effect shows this only for visible and ultraviolet light.
items.why: The photoelectric effect is taught with visible and ultraviolet light and Compton scattering with X-rays, so the two experiments are filed as covering different parts of the spectrum rather than as testing different properties (energy and momentum) of the same photon. Ask what each experiment measures: the photoelectric effect tests the photon's energy hf, Compton scattering tests its momentum h/λ. Both apply across the spectrum; the new evidence from Compton scattering is about momentum, not about which radiation counts as photons.
items.specStatementText: Compton scattering of light by electrons as additional evidence of the particle nature of light
items.random_wrong: X-rays are scattered in every direction by the electrons in the target, which a wave could not do, so the X-rays must be particles.

items.q: An X-ray photon of wavelength 2.20 × 10⁻¹¹ m is scattered by a free electron that is initially at rest. The scattered photon has wavelength 2.60 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the kinetic energy of the recoiling electron?
items.why:
The photoelectric effect is met first and its rule 'the electron gets the photon's energy hf' is carried over; the scattered photon is then thought of as a separate, newly emitted photon that does not enter the energy account. Keep the two processes apart. Photoelectric: photon absorbed, E_max = hf − Φ. Compton: photon scattered, so energy conservation reads hc/λ_i = hc/λ_f + E_k(electron).

Working: Incident photon energy E_i = hc/λ_i = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(2.20 × 10⁻¹¹ m) = 9.04 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. Scattered photon energy E_f = hc/λ_f = (1.989 × 10⁻²⁵ J m)/(2.60 × 10⁻¹¹ m) = 7.65 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. Energy is conserved and the electron starts at rest, so E_k = E_i − E_f = 9.04 × 10⁻¹⁵ − 7.65 × 10⁻¹⁵ = 1.39 × 10⁻¹⁵ J (about 8.7 keV). The shift of 4.0 × 10⁻¹² m is less than the maximum Compton shift 2h/m_e c = 4.85 × 10⁻¹² m, so the data are physically possible.

items.q: Do all photoelectrons released by light of one frequency leave the metal with the same kinetic energy, hf − Φ?
items.correct: No. They leave with a range of kinetic energies from zero up to a maximum, E_max = hf − Φ.
items.misconception: Every photon gives the same energy hf and every electron needs Φ to escape, so every photoelectron has kinetic energy exactly hf − Φ.
items.why: The equation is often written or remembered without the 'max', and students treat the work function as the energy every electron needs rather than the minimum energy needed by the least tightly held electrons. Φ is the MINIMUM energy needed to remove an electron. Electrons below the surface lose extra energy in collisions on the way out, so they leave with less than hf − Φ. The equation gives only the maximum kinetic energy, which is why a stopping potential that stops the fastest electrons measures E_max.
items.specStatementText: Einstein’s explanation using the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons as given by E_max = hf − Φ where Φ is the work function of the metal
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the stopping potential a measure of the work function of the metal?
items.correct: No. The stopping potential measures the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons: eV_s = E_max = hf − Φ. The work function is the energy needed to release the electron in the first place.
items.misconception: The stopping potential is the potential that holds electrons in the metal, so eV_s equals the work function Φ.
items.why: Both the work function and the stopping potential are described as 'barriers' that hold back electrons, and both are quoted in eV or V, so students merge the two quantities and also confuse them with E_max. The work function acts at the surface and is overcome by the photon's energy. The stopping potential acts between the plate and the collector on electrons that have already escaped, and it measures how much kinetic energy the fastest of them have: eV_s = E_max. Only if the same light is used can one be found from the other, using E_max = hf − Φ.
items.specStatementText: Einstein’s explanation using the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons as given by E_max = hf − Φ where Φ is the work function of the metal

items.q: In Einstein's photoelectric equation, is the work function added to the photon energy?
items.correct: No. The work function is energy the electron must USE to escape, so it is subtracted: E_max = hf − Φ.
items.misconception: The work function is energy the metal gives to the electron as it leaves, so the maximum kinetic energy is hf + Φ.
items.why: The word 'work' suggests work done ON the electron, supplying energy, rather than work the electron must do against the attraction of the metal. Sign conventions for work done on and by a system are a documented general difficulty. The electron is attracted back towards the metal, so it must do work against that attraction to escape. Energy conservation gives hf = Φ + E_max, so E_max = hf − Φ, which is always less than the photon energy.
items.specStatementText: Einstein’s explanation using the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons as given by E_max = hf − Φ where Φ is the work function of the metal
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a larger potential difference across a photocell always give a larger photocurrent, as in Ohm's law?
items.correct: No. Once the collector is positive enough to collect every photoelectron, the current reaches a saturation value set by the number of photoelectrons emitted per second, which depends on the intensity of the light.
items.misconception: The current in a photocell is set by the potential difference across it, as for a resistor, so at a given potential difference the current does not depend on the light.
items.why: Students' main model of current comes from circuits with resistors, where I = V/R, and they apply it to the photocell, reading its current–potential graph as if it were the characteristic of a resistor. In a photocell the charge carriers are the photoelectrons released by the light. The potential difference only decides what fraction of them reach the collector. The saturation current equals the charge of all the photoelectrons emitted per second, and it doubles if the intensity (number of photons per second) doubles.
items.specStatementText: Einstein’s explanation using the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons as given by E_max = hf − Φ where Φ is the work function of the metal

items.q: Can an energy in joules be compared with, or subtracted from, an energy in electronvolts without converting?
items.correct: No. Both energies must be in the same unit: 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
items.misconception: Numbers for energy can be combined directly whatever their unit, so a photon energy in joules can be compared with a work function in eV, or an energy in eV can be used as if it were in joules.
items.why: Quantum physics problems mix J and eV, and photon energies calculated from hc/λ come out in joules while work functions are quoted in eV. Students focusing on the formula overlook the units. Convert before combining: an energy in eV is multiplied by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ to give joules. For example, 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.91 eV. A kinetic energy used in p = √(2mE_k) must be in joules.
items.specStatementText: Einstein’s explanation using the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons as given by E_max = hf − Φ where Φ is the work function of the metal

items.q: Does diffraction, or the first minimum of a diffraction pattern, occur only when the wavelength equals the size of the gap or obstacle?
items.correct: No. Diffraction is significant when the wavelength is comparable with the size of the object, and the first minimum occurs at an angle given by sin θ ≈ λ/D, which depends on the ratio of λ to D.
items.misconception: Diffraction happens when the wavelength is equal to the size of the gap or object, so the size of the object is simply equal to the wavelength.
items.why: Introductory courses state that diffraction is greatest 'when the gap is the same size as the wavelength', and students turn a rough comparison into an equation. The angle of the first minimum depends on λ/D: sin θ ≈ λ/D. If λ = D the first minimum would be at 90°. Measuring the angle of the first minimum and using D ≈ λ/sin θ gives the size of the object.
items.specStatementText: diffraction of particles as evidence of the wave nature of matter

items.q: Once the wave nature of electrons is accepted, is an electron simply a spread-out classical wave?
items.correct: No. An electron shows wave behaviour in how it propagates and interferes, but it is always detected at a single point, as a particle.
items.misconception: An electron is really a wave spread out in space, like a ripple, and the particle description no longer applies; its charge is smeared over the wave.
items.why: After learning about electron diffraction students sometimes replace the particle model with a classical wave model instead of holding both, just as they previously held a particle-only model. Each electron is detected at one place, with its whole charge and mass. Its wave behaviour appears in the statistics of many detections, which show interference. Duality means neither classical model alone is adequate.
items.specStatementText: that matter exhibits wave–particle duality
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do two particles with the same kinetic energy move at the same speed?
items.correct: No. E_k = ½mv², so for equal kinetic energy the lighter particle moves faster: v ∝ 1/√m.
items.misconception: Equal kinetic energy means equal speed, so two particles with the same kinetic energy differ only in mass, and λ = h/mv is inversely proportional to mass.
items.why: In everyday language 'energetic' and 'fast' are used as if they mean the same thing, and students hold one variable fixed in λ = h/mv without checking whether it changes. At equal kinetic energy, p = √(2mE_k) ∝ √m, so λ = h/p ∝ 1/√m. A particle 1830 times more massive has √1830 ≈ 43 times the momentum and 1/43 of the wavelength, not 1/1830.
items.specStatementText: the de Broglie wavelength for particles as given by λ = h/p
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is visible light made of photons, or only high-frequency radiation such as X-rays and gamma rays?
items.correct: All electromagnetic radiation consists of photons, including visible light and radio waves; the energy of each photon is hf.
items.misconception: Only high-frequency radiation such as X-rays and gamma rays behaves as photons; visible light is purely a wave.
items.why: Visible light is studied through interference, diffraction and refraction, while photons are introduced with X-rays, gamma rays and radioactivity, so students attach 'particle' only to high-energy radiation. The photoelectric effect itself is observed with visible and ultraviolet light, and Einstein's photon explanation applies to all frequencies. Low-frequency photons simply carry less energy, E = hf.
items.specStatementText: Compton scattering of light by electrons as additional evidence of the particle nature of light

items.q: Is the longer wavelength of Compton-scattered X-rays caused by the beam becoming weaker?
items.correct: No. The wavelength of each scattered photon is longer because that photon has less energy. The intensity of the beam does not affect the wavelength.
items.misconception: Some photons are absorbed or lost, so the scattered beam is less intense, and a weaker beam has a longer wavelength.
items.why: Students link energy, intensity and wavelength loosely and treat 'less energy in the beam' and 'less energy per photon' as the same thing, the same confusion between intensity and photon energy found in the photoelectric effect. The number of photons sets the intensity; the energy of each photon sets its wavelength (E = hc/λ). A single photon scattered by a single electron has a longer wavelength because it gave some of its own energy to that electron.

items.q: Does the Compton shift Δλ depend on the incident wavelength?
items.correct: No. Δλ = (h/m_e c)(1 − cos θ) depends only on the scattering angle. For a given angle the shift is the same for any incident wavelength.
items.misconception: The Compton shift is proportional to the incident wavelength: the scattered wavelength is longer by a fixed fraction of the incident wavelength.
items.why: Students expect a change in a quantity to be a fixed fraction of its original value, as in the Doppler effect for light, where Δλ/λ ≈ v/c, so they assume a longer incident wavelength gives a proportionally longer shift. The formula contains no λ_i: the same angle gives the same Δλ, at most 2h/m_e c ≈ 4.9 × 10⁻¹² m. What depends on the incident wavelength is the FRACTIONAL change Δλ/λ_i, which is significant for X-rays (λ about 10⁻¹¹ m) and negligible for visible light (λ about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m).
items.specStatementText: the shift in photon wavelength after scattering off an electron as given by λ_f − λ_i = Δλ = (h/m_e c)(1 − cos θ).
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the Compton formula, is the angle factor cos θ?
items.correct: No. The factor is (1 − cos θ), which is zero at θ = 0° and greatest, 2, at θ = 180°.
items.misconception: The shift is (h/m_e c) cos θ, so it is greatest for photons that continue straight on (θ = 0°) and negative beyond 90°.
items.why: The '1 −' is easily dropped when the formula is recalled or keyed into a calculator, and many other physics formulas contain a plain cos θ. At θ = 0° the photon is not deflected and nothing happens to it, so the shift must be zero, which requires the factor 1 − cos θ. The shift then increases steadily to its maximum, 2h/m_e c, at 180°.
items.specStatementText: the shift in photon wavelength after scattering off an electron as given by λ_f − λ_i = Δλ = (h/m_e c)(1 − cos θ).
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the Compton shift always equal to h/m_e c?
items.correct: No. h/m_e c = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m is the constant in the formula; the shift is (h/m_e c)(1 − cos θ), which varies from zero to 2h/m_e c with the angle.
items.misconception: The shift in wavelength is a fixed amount, h/m_e c, for every scattered photon, whatever the angle.
items.why: The quantity h/m_e c is given a name (the Compton wavelength) and a single value, so students take it to be the shift itself. The shift depends on the scattering angle through (1 − cos θ): zero at 0°, h/m_e c at 90° and 2h/m_e c at 180°.

items.q: Can a calculator left in radian mode be used for angles given in degrees?
items.correct: No. The calculator must be in degree mode when the angle is in degrees; cos 120° = −0.50, whereas cos(120 rad) = 0.81.
items.misconception: The trigonometric functions give the same value whatever mode the calculator is in, so the mode need not be checked.
items.why: Calculators keep their last mode, and students rarely check it; a radian-mode result looks like any other number. Always check the calculator mode against the unit of the angle, and check that the result is reasonable: sin 51° is about 0.78, and 1 − cos 120° is 1.5.

items.q: Does Compton scattering show that photons have mass?
items.correct: No. A photon has zero rest mass but still carries momentum p = h/λ = E/c. Compton scattering shows that this momentum is real: it is exchanged with the electron, and momentum is conserved in the collision.
items.misconception: Photons must have mass, because momentum is mv and only a particle with mass can carry momentum into a collision.
items.why: Momentum is introduced as p = mv, so momentum without mass seems impossible; the billiard-ball picture used to describe Compton scattering reinforces the idea of a small massive ball. For a photon, p = h/λ (equivalently E/c). Momentum is a property carried by waves and fields as well as by massive particles, and a photon, with zero rest mass, has it.
items.specStatementText: Compton scattering of light by electrons as additional evidence of the particle nature of light

items.q: If a photon's wavelength increases by Δλ, is the energy it loses equal to hc/Δλ?
items.correct: No. Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, so a difference in wavelength does not convert to a difference in energy by the same formula. The energy lost is hc/λ_i − hc/λ_f, found from the two wavelengths separately.
items.misconception: Because E = hc/λ, a change in wavelength Δλ corresponds to a change in energy hc/Δλ.
items.why: Formulae met earlier (E = hf, Δp = FΔt) are linear, so 'apply the formula to the change' works; a small Δλ substituted into hc/Δλ gives a very large number, which is not recognized as impossible. Calculate each photon energy first, then subtract: ΔE = hc(1/λ_i − 1/λ_f). Check the size: the electron cannot receive more than the incident photon's whole energy hc/λ_i.
items.specStatementText: that photons scatter off electrons with increased wavelength

items.q: Is the energy of a photon given by h/λ?
items.correct: No. h/λ is the photon's MOMENTUM, in kg m s⁻¹. Its energy is hf = hc/λ, in joules.
items.misconception: The energy of a photon is h/λ.
items.why: E = hf and p = h/λ both pair Planck's constant with a wave quantity, and the two are merged into one formula; the factor c that links them is dropped. Check the unit: h/λ has units J s m⁻¹ = kg m s⁻¹, a momentum. Energy needs a further factor of c: E = pc = hc/λ.
